scores.helpfulness_justification: Both sides gained something (Northwind the 8% S2 limit and 6-year retrofit; Halcyon the 36-month S4 date and a flexible S5 remedy), and the F gap is only 1.

instances.excerpt: 55 °C test, but the maximum failure rate is 8% with no phase-in; customers receive per-model results confidentially; the regulator receives results; no public disclosure.
instances.comparison: The key allows a permanent limit of 5% and an interim limit of at most 7%. A permanent 8% limit is weakened. It exempts Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%). The customer disclosure of per-model results is sound, and there is no retest requirement for models already on sale within 12 months, though retesting every 3 years is required.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Report fire, uncontrolled overheating, injury or material property damage within 72 hours; customers notified within 5 business days of determining action is needed; underreporting must be disclosed and investigated.
S1_incident_reporting.comparison: The 72-hour serious-incident window is at the edge of the acceptable range. The scope is narrower than the key, since 'material property damage' excludes minor smoke or overheating. No separate 30-day window for other incidents is set, and customer notice is within 5 business days, which is within the ≤45-day range. Overall it is within acceptable bounds and not clearly weakened.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report any thermal incident involving fire, uncontrolled overheating, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. A preliminary report may be updated as facts are confirmed. The manufacturer must promptly notify affected customers when an incident presents a credible safety risk, and in any event within 5 business days of determining that customer action is needed. Reports must include known incident counts and corrective actions; suspected underreporting must be disclosed and investigated.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: 55 °C test, but the maximum failure rate is 8% with no phase-in; customers receive per-model results confidentially; the regulator receives results; no public disclosure.
S2_thermal_testing.comparison: The key allows a permanent limit of 5% and an interim limit of at most 7%. A permanent 8% limit is weakened. It exempts Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%). The customer disclosure of per-model results is sound, and there is no retest requirement for models already on sale within 12 months, though retesting every 3 years is required.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before initial sale, at least every 3 years, and after a material design or manufacturing change. No model may be sold if more than 8% of tested units fail; the manufacturer must take corrective action and pass retesting before sale resumes. Manufacturers must provide per-model test protocols, results, and failure rates confidentially to the relevant regulator. Customers and prospective customers must be given the test results and failure rate for the specific model they are considering or have purchased, in a clear and timely manner. Customer disclosure does not require public disclosure of other models’ results.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units must support remote shut-off from 12 months; installed units that lack it get an upgrade or replacement pathway completed within 6 years, where technically feasible.
S3_remote_shutoff.comparison: This is within the acceptable range (new units within 12 months, retrofit within 7 years). The 'where technically feasible' qualifier is a mild loophole, and there is no prioritisation of higher-risk units. It favours Northwind relative to the 3-year safe benchmark.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: All new home battery units must support remote emergency shut-off beginning 12 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers must enable remote shut-off for installed units that support the capability and provide customers clear instructions within 12 months. For installed units lacking the capability, manufacturers must provide an upgrade or replacement pathway and complete it within 6 years, where technically feasible. Shut-off must be performed only when necessary to address an imminent safety risk, with prompt notice to affected customers when practicable.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: Built-in fire suppression is required on new units from 36 months after adoption, with no retrofit.
S4_fire_suppression.comparison: This is within the acceptable range (≤48 months) but later than the safe 24 months. It meets HC-2.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: All new home battery units manufactured for sale must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. Before that date, manufacturers must provide installation and maintenance instructions that support safe operation and must disclose whether the unit includes built-in suppression. The requirement applies to units manufactured on or after the effective date; it does not require retrofitting units already installed.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: Recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units per year; the regulator sets a proportionate remedy, with no automatic permanent sales ban; interim protective measures are allowed; customers are notified promptly.
S5_customer_disclosure.comparison: The numeric 8/100k trigger is mandatory, matching the key. The remedy flexibility softens it, so Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9) can stay on the market with corrective action. The customer notice window is 'promptly' rather than a fixed 14 or 30 days, which is vague. There is no specified interim phase-in. This is mostly acceptable but leans soft.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers with clear safety information at purchase, including safe installation and use, warning signs, emergency steps, and a contact route for reporting incidents. Customers must be notified promptly when new information indicates a material risk or requires inspection, repair, software action, or other safety action. Regulators must assess model-level thermal incident rates using verified reports and a stated denominator and period. A recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. The regulator shall set a proportionate recall remedy, which may include repair, replacement, software action, or removal from service; exceeding the trigger alone does not require a permanent sales ban if an effective corrective action is available. Regulators may require interim protective measures while investigating.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: The evidence favors keeping S2 test failure rates and S5 incident rates as separate, model-level measures: Halcyon’s flagship is at 3.9% on the 55°C test but 9.9 thermal incidents per 100,000 units, while Northwind’s Hearth 10 is at 6.2% and 6.4 incidents per 100,000, respectively. A mandatory S5 trigger should use verified model-level incidents, installed-unit denominators, and a defined annual period; company-wide averages should not obscure a model exceeding the trigger. Regulators can verify the data and require interim protective measures.

judge_section_notes: The final rules stay within the red lines of both companies. The main weakening is S2's 8% permanent failure limit with no phase-in, which lets Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%) stay on sale. S5 keeps the 8/100k recall trigger but lets the regulator choose a remedy, which protects Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9) from an automatic ban. S1, S3 and S4 are within the acceptable ranges.
